frictionVectors.title: European Gas Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while pressing for more flexible supply and investment terms. Algeria retains strong state control but remains exposed to hydrocarbon-market volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's non-intervention posture. Competing Russian, Western, and regional influence raises pressure on Algiers.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is attracting strong US, European, and Chinese interest because of its access to Central African minerals. Angola can gain leverage, but financing and operating dependence may dilute national control.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: External debt obligations and declining oil output constrain fiscal autonomy. International lenders and energy firms retain substantial influence over infrastructure and production decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Export Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Niger oil-export route through Benin remains vulnerable to diplomatic tensions and border restrictions. Pipeline and port infrastructure provide leverage but also expose Benin to regional retaliation.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's trade and logistics networks rely heavily on external financiers, regional commerce, and foreign operators. Chinese and Western infrastructure interests compete for influence over future expansion.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater value capture and domestic beneficiation as the diamond market weakens. The dispute tests its ability to preserve control while retaining foreign marketing and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Positioning
frictionVectors.details: New mineral opportunities could diversify the economy, but development will require external capital and infrastructure. Botswana is seeking partnerships without sacrificing its established regulatory autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgent Pressure on Mining
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity threatens gold-producing areas, transport routes, and state revenue collection. Security constraints limit the government's ability to translate resource-nationalist policies into durable control.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer reliance on Russian security assistance reduces Western influence but creates new dependency risks. Changes to foreign mining arrangements and gold governance may trigger legal, financial, and diplomatic retaliation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mineral Chains
frictionVectors.details: Gold and nickel projects attract Chinese and regional investors while weak oversight and informal exports limit Burundi's ability to capture value. The government is seeking tighter licensing and local-processing requirements.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent political distrust with Rwanda complicates cross-border commerce and security coordination. Limited domestic electricity generation keeps Burundi dependent on regional power imports and external finance.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European, Chinese, and other external partners compete for influence around ports, logistics, fisheries, and maritime surveillance. Cabo Verde is using this competition to strengthen its bargaining position while avoiding excessive dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Water Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains vulnerable to imported fuel, desalination costs, and climate-driven water stress. Renewable-energy investment is improving resilience but still relies heavily on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign contractors remain deeply involved in roads, ports, dams, and mining, creating financing and debt-exposure concerns. Infrastructure development expands state capacity but often provides limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Separatist and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest regions disrupts transport, agriculture, and public revenue. Instability along the Nigerian and Central African Republic borders also complicates control of trade and resource corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-for-Resources Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian security personnel and political backing has strengthened regime survival but narrowed independent control over mining concessions and export channels. Gold and diamond governance remains vulnerable to opaque arrangements and smuggling.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and weak state administration continue to disrupt roads linking Bangui with Cameroon, Chad, and Sudan. Dependence on neighboring transit infrastructure leaves the country exposed to external political and security pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Chad's strategic position keeps it important to European, regional, and Gulf security actors, but external military relationships can limit policy autonomy. The government is balancing demands for sovereignty with continued reliance on outside intelligence, finance, and equipment.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Public finances remain highly exposed to oil prices, production disruptions, and the export route through Cameroon. Foreign operators and creditors retain substantial leverage over the sector, while conflict and instability around Sudan threaten alternative trade corridors.

highlights: Ports and connectivity remain externally dependent

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros territorial dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration enforcement and maritime jurisdiction generate recurring diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited fiscal capacity leaves port, telecommunications, and energy development reliant on foreign partners, constraining independent resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–M23 conflict
frictionVectors.details: Fighting in the east continues to undermine state control over territory and mineral routes, with Kinshasa accusing Rwanda of supporting M23 and Kigali citing security threats.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper bargaining imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a dominant position in processing, infrastructure, and mining finance, while the government seeks stronger contract terms and greater domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on offshore oil exposes Brazzaville to price volatility and limits diversification, while foreign operators retain substantial technical and commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects expand connectivity but can constrain fiscal autonomy through repayment obligations and preferential commercial access.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa processing and price exposure
frictionVectors.details: The government is expanding domestic processing and producer support, but multinational buyers and volatile global prices still limit national control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign competition around ports and energy
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and other investors compete for influence over Abidjan logistics and power infrastructure, creating leverage opportunities but also strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: The presence of US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generates substantial revenue but limits Djibouti's room to maneuver in regional crises.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports and rail links are central to Ethiopia's trade, yet debt exposure and foreign control of major infrastructure create persistent sovereignty and repayment risks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and strategic-asset dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs leave Cairo dependent on Gulf investment, IMF support, and asset monetization. This constrains policy autonomy around ports, logistics, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Instability around the Red Sea threatens Suez Canal revenues, while the unresolved Nile dam dispute with Ethiopia remains a core sovereignty concern. Egypt is expanding diplomatic and military partnerships to protect water and maritime interests.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field production and limited diversification increase dependence on foreign operators, LNG infrastructure, and external technical capital. The state retains formal ownership but has diminishing leverage over the sector's future.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque external financing
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and security relationships remain important as Malabo seeks infrastructure and revenue alternatives. Debt opacity and weak governance reduce the developmental returns of strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: Port access and regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Assab and Massawa give Eritrea outsized strategic value, but competition among Gulf, Turkish, Egyptian, and other regional actors raises pressure over access and alignment. Tensions with Ethiopia continue to make border and maritime infrastructure highly sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but depend on foreign operators and external markets. International scrutiny over labor practices and sanctions risk complicates efforts to convert mineral wealth into sovereign development.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal exposure to South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Customs receipts, electricity imports, transport links, and access to South African markets underpin Eswatini's economic stability. Any slowdown or policy shift in Pretoria would quickly narrow Mbabane's fiscal room.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy and investment risk
frictionVectors.details: Continued political restrictions and periodic unrest complicate efforts to attract diversified foreign investment. External partners generally prioritize stability and commercial access while avoiding direct confrontation over governance.

highlights: Debt and Red Sea access remain contested

frictionVectors.title: Nile water confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam has increased Addis Ababa's control over national power and water infrastructure, but Egypt and Sudan still seek binding operating guarantees. The dispute remains vulnerable to escalation during drought or wider regional crises.

frictionVectors.title: Debt, ports, and external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and the search for reliable Red Sea access expose Ethiopia to competing Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional agendas. Any port or corridor arrangement will carry major sovereignty implications alongside significant economic benefits.

highlights: Military transition tightens control over mining and oil
Manganese diplomacy balances France, China and Gulf investors

frictionVectors.title: Resource renegotiation risk
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing for greater state participation and local processing in manganese and hydrocarbons. This may improve sovereign capture but risks disputes with established foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors linking mines to Owendo and other coastal facilities remain vulnerable to financing and operational dependence on external partners, particularly Chinese and European firms.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential security and economic partner
Cashew, fisheries and port access shape sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional connectivity, trade routes and security cooperation. This supports stability but limits policy autonomy around borders, fisheries and transport.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing pressure and limited maritime enforcement weaken national control over marine resources. Port modernization and external investment could improve capacity while creating new leverage for outside actors.

highlights: Gold and emerging lithium sectors test local-value rules

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and environmentally damaging mining continues to erode state control over gold revenues and land. Foreign-linked buying networks and informal exports complicate enforcement despite stronger local-processing ambitions.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more domestic value addition in lithium and other minerals while facing pressure from international investors and creditors for predictable, bankable rules. Infrastructure and fiscal constraints limit its negotiating leverage.

highlights: Bauxite and Simandou reshape Guinea's strategic weight
Junta-led resource nationalism faces execution constraints

frictionVectors.title: Simandou external concentration
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is dominated by large foreign consortia and depends on extensive rail and port infrastructure. The state may gain major revenues, but financing, ownership and export logistics create substantial external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite corridor tensions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked investment remains central to bauxite production and transport, while the authorities demand more processing and state participation. Social grievances, land impacts and opaque contracting could undermine claims of sovereign control.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy exposed
Political fragility weakens control of ports and borders

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign buyers, seasonal price shocks and limited domestic processing. This keeps value capture largely outside Guinea-Bissau.

frictionVectors.title: Port and trafficking vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political tensions reduce effective control over ports, maritime space and border crossings. The resulting environment facilitates illicit networks and gives external commercial and security actors disproportionate influence.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF requirements and substantial Chinese and commercial debt limit Nairobi's fiscal room. Public resistance to tax increases and austerity complicates efforts to preserve sovereign control over infrastructure and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Contest
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and transport corridor remain exposed to security risks and competing Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests. Regional instability could delay Kenya's bid to become an autonomous logistics hub.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's fiscal position and infrastructure planning remain heavily tied to water exports to South Africa under the Lesotho Highlands Water Project. Delays, cost overruns, and unequal bargaining power constrain national control over the resource.

frictionVectors.title: Hydropower Financing
frictionVectors.details: New hydropower and transmission projects require substantial external finance, increasing dependence on South African institutions and international lenders. Climate variability also threatens the reliability of water and electricity revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other projects are attracting foreign capital, but Liberia remains dependent on concession agreements for exports, jobs, and infrastructure. Weak enforcement capacity risks leaving the state with limited value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and investors retain major influence over port logistics and mining-linked transport corridors. Monrovia is seeking stronger local revenue and regulatory control without deterring badly needed investment.

frictionVectors.title: Rival Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities and armed groups continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, terminals, and revenue flows. Foreign energy partnerships and security ties reinforce fragmented rather than unified sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mediterranean Influence Race
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the UAE, and European states compete for military, energy, migration, and reconstruction leverage. External support gives local factions bargaining power while limiting a coherent national infrastructure strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining projects in nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and graphite provide exports and infrastructure but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles and uneven fiscal returns. Governance disputes continue over land, environmental damage, and local benefit sharing.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Ports and logistics infrastructure attract Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western interest because of Madagascar's position in the western Indian Ocean. Limited state capacity makes long-term control of strategic facilities a recurring sovereignty concern.

highlights: Mining sector opens under external capital

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Revenue Control
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign investment in uranium, rare earths and other minerals while facing pressure to improve licensing transparency and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fuel imports, electricity shortages and reliance on external financing leave critical infrastructure vulnerable to donor, lender and regional supply pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Nationalism and Contract Revision
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is tightening control over gold production and challenging established mining arrangements, increasing friction with foreign operators while state capacity remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security and External Alignment
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal from Western security frameworks and reliance on Russian-linked forces have reduced Western leverage but intensified sanctions, insecurity and infrastructure risk.

highlights: Gas era begins amid foreign partnerships

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major export potential but ties Mauritania to multinational operators, Senegalese coordination and complex revenue-management demands.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports and planned green-hydrogen projects depend heavily on foreign capital, port capacity and transport corridors, limiting near-term domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty dispute over the Chagos Archipelago and the future of the Diego Garcia military facility remains Mauritius's principal external-security and diplomatic pressure point.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime and Financial Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius depends on open sea lanes, international finance and external tourism markets, creating vulnerability to geopolitical shocks despite strong institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of Western Sahara and its phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy assets continues to generate diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front and some international partners.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, rail, renewable energy and industrial projects draw substantial European, Gulf and Chinese interest, strengthening capacity while creating competing external leverage.

highlights: Cabo Delgado remains the key constraint

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG dominance
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies retain major control over liquefied natural gas financing, technology, and market access. Maputo is seeking greater domestic participation while needing foreign capital to restart delayed projects.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten LNG infrastructure and local legitimacy in the gas-producing north. External military and security support remains important to protecting strategic assets.

highlights: Green hydrogen ambitions face execution risk

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of new hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Recent oil and gas discoveries have attracted major international operators, creating pressure for stronger local-content and state-participation rules. Namibia is attempting to convert exploration interest into durable sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Green-hydrogen infrastructure gap
frictionVectors.details: Large projects depend on external finance, export buyers, and imported technology. Weak domestic grid and port capacity could leave Namibia capturing less value than headline investment figures suggest.

highlights: Junta asserts control over strategic resources
Sanctions and isolation narrow operating space

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and foreign-company disputes
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control over uranium and other extractive assets while renegotiating or challenging longstanding foreign operating arrangements. The confrontation risks reduced production, legal disputes, and lost export revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports rely on cross-border infrastructure and regional access that remain vulnerable to political rupture and insecurity. Dependence on external partners limits the junta's practical sovereignty despite its assertive rhetoric.

highlights: Power and logistics constrain industrial sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: International oil dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators, international lenders, and commodity markets still shape Nigeria's upstream investment and export earnings. Production reforms may improve state revenue, but local refining and value capture remain uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and gas bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity, gas-supply constraints, and transmission shortfalls limit domestic processing and manufacturing. Foreign-backed infrastructure can relieve bottlenecks but also deepen dependence on external finance and technology.

highlights: Regional security posture draws external scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals supply chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda has built influence as a regional minerals-trading and processing hub, but its supply chains face persistent scrutiny over traceability and links to conflict-affected eastern Congo. External buyers and standards bodies retain significant leverage.

frictionVectors.title: External security partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's military role in regional conflicts and overseas security deployments generates diplomatic friction and potential sanctions exposure. These partnerships enhance Kigali's bargaining power while increasing dependence on external political and financial relationships.

highlights: China ties deepen after Taiwan switch

frictionVectors.title: Offshore licensing uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in São Tomé and Príncipe’s maritime zone has yet to produce commercially viable output, leaving the state vulnerable to unfavorable future concessions. Limited technical and financial capacity constrains sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea fisheries pressure
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing threatens coastal livelihoods and weakens control over the country’s maritime resources. São Tomé relies heavily on external partners for surveillance and enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Contract renegotiation risk
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value and transparency from oil and gas projects, including Sangomar and the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim development. Renegotiation could improve state capture but may unsettle investors and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas-border coordination
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania gas project requires sustained cross-border coordination on revenue, infrastructure and security. Delays or disputes could reduce expected fiscal benefits and increase dependence on foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Tuna access and fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fleets and access agreements remain central to Seychelles’ fisheries economy, creating recurring tension over licensing revenue, local processing and enforcement. The country lacks the capacity to fully police its extensive maritime zone.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China and other partners compete for influence through maritime security, port and connectivity projects. Seychelles must balance these relationships while avoiding excessive strategic or debt dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Large-scale mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile and other mineral projects generate essential revenue but expose the state to concession asymmetries, environmental damage and limited domestic value addition. Chinese and other foreign-linked operators remain significant in the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Freetown’s port and transport infrastructure require foreign capital, creating opportunities for outside influence over strategic logistics. Debt, concession terms and local employment benefits remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Somaliland and Red Sea rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The dispute over Somaliland’s external security and port relationships, including Ethiopia’s search for Red Sea access, directly challenges Mogadishu’s territorial sovereignty. Gulf, Turkish and Western interests amplify the strategic stakes.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore hydrocarbons under insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil ambitions are advancing amid weak enforcement capacity, contested maritime claims and the persistent threat from al-Shabaab. Foreign security and energy partners are therefore positioned to capture a substantial share of future value.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial platinum, manganese and chrome resources, but limited domestic processing and infrastructure constraints leave value chains exposed to foreign capital and external markets.

frictionVectors.title: Power-sector vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Eskom reliability and transmission shortages continue to constrain industrial sovereignty, while private and foreign-backed generation increasingly fills the gap.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export chokepoint
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese pipelines and Port Sudan for most oil exports, leaving national revenue hostage to conflict, transit disruptions and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Political and armed networks compete for oil revenues, land and border trade, while neighboring states and international actors retain significant influence over security and economic access.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and war financing
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain central to financing rival armed structures, with regional trading networks and foreign buyers weakening effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Conflict around transport corridors, Port Sudan and oil infrastructure threatens export capacity and increases dependence on external security, logistics and humanitarian actors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater state participation and local value addition in gold, nickel and critical-mineral projects, but remains reliant on foreign financing, technology and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Dar es Salaam port and regional rail corridors are gaining strategic importance, drawing competition among Gulf, Chinese, Western and neighboring-state interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port-centered external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's port and logistics networks are vital to regional trade but depend heavily on foreign operators, finance and security partnerships, limiting domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate processing gap
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains significant phosphate resources, yet incomplete downstream processing and exposure to international commodity markets constrain sovereign value capture.

highlights: State tightens control over strategic sectors

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European cooperation on migration, budget support, and trade remains a major source of external leverage. Tunis resists political conditionality while still relying on European markets and assistance.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and reliance on imported gas constrain Tunisia's strategic autonomy. Phosphate disruption and underinvestment in renewables further pressure the state-owned energy system.

highlights: Oil development advances toward first exports

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and environmental opposition
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to planned petroleum revenues but faces international criticism, financing constraints, and displacement concerns. Foreign operators retain major influence over project execution and future export flows.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external lenders remain important to transport and energy construction. Debt-service obligations reduce Kampala's flexibility in allocating future commodity revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: New investment from Gulf, Chinese, and Western-linked firms is expanding copper capacity, but Zambia still exports much of its mineral output with limited domestic processing. Fiscal and ownership terms remain politically contested.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: The corridor offers an alternative route for copper exports and reduces dependence on southern routes, but its financing, logistics, and mineral access are increasingly tied to external strategic interests.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing foreign partners

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mineral licensing competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in lithium and other mineral projects, while Western and regional actors seek greater access. Zimbabwe's beneficiation policies have increased state leverage but have not yet created broad domestic value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chronic power shortages constrain mining and manufacturing, forcing reliance on imports, private generation, and external infrastructure providers. Energy weakness limits the government's ability to capture more value from strategic minerals.
